problem: The answer describes the leakage direction wrongly: a random row split does not put only later values in train and earlier values in test. It scatters both early and late points across both sets, so training rows end up later in time than many test rows. As written, a student may think random splitting always puts the future in train and the past in test, which is not what happens.
fix: Say: random rows scatter early and late points across both sets, so training contains values recorded after some test values. The model is effectively shown the future of those test points. Correct split: sort by time, train on the earlier segment, test on the later segment, and keep windows from crossing the boundary.

problem: The answer rejects seq2seq on the ground that the output is 'not a new sequence of different length'. Length equality is not the distinguishing feature; seq2seq can produce an output of the same length as the input. The real reason is that each output tag is tied to one input position.
fix: Say: this is many-to-many labelling with the same length, because each input word gets one tag at the same step, so T input words give T aligned output tags. It is not seq2seq because the outputs are aligned one-to-one with the inputs, not generated as a separate sequence.
